s: harmonium use free reed (construction principle imported from China)
q: For instance, the _free reed_ used in the harmonium is an importation from China.

s: Kratzenstein applies harmonium (about the end of the last century)
q: The organ builder Kratzenstein, who lived in St. Petersburg during the reign of Catharine II., happened to see the Chinese instrument _cheng_, which is of this construction, and it suggested to him, about the end of the last century, to apply the _free reed_ to certain organ stops.

s: harmonium compete with pianoforte (as a universal favourite in western Europe)
q: At the present day instruments of the harmonium class have become such universal favourites in western Europe as almost to compete with the pianoforte.

s: pianoforte develop from dulcimer (prototype)
q: The prototype of our pianoforte was evidently the dulcimer, known at an early time to the Arabs and Persians who call it _santir_.

s: musical instruments use material metal (common construction material)
q: Wood, metal, and the hide of animals, are the most common substances used in the construction of musical instruments.

s: dulcimer is called cimbalom (by Magyars in Hungary)
q: The Poles at the present day call it _cymbaly_, and the Magyars in Hungary _cimbalom_.

s: pianoforte develop from clavicembalo (the clavicembalo was its predecessor)
q: The _clavicembalo_, the predecessor of the pianoforte, was in fact nothing but a _cembalo_ with a key-board attached to it;

s: dulcimer possess strings (in its primitive form, stretched across a wooden board)
q: Again, the gradual development of the dulcimer from a rude contrivance, consisting merely of a wooden board across which a few strings are stretched, is distinctly traceable by a reference to the musical instruments of nations in different stages of civilization.

s: harp develop from elastic stick bent by a string (inferred primitive form)
q: We might perhaps infer from its shape that it originally consisted of nothing more than an elastic stick bent by a string.

s: harp develop toward greater constructional improvement (through instruments with sound-boards and multiple strings)
q: In short, the more improved we find these contrivances the closer they approach our harp.

s: South Kensington collection contain instruments from Egypt and western Asia (still in use and resembling ancient monument representations)
q: At South Kensington may be seen instruments still in use in Egypt and western Asia, precisely like specimens represented on monuments dating from a period of three thousand years ago.

s: Egypt possess ancient musical instruments (still in use and resembling instruments on monuments)
q: At South Kensington may be seen instruments still in use in Egypt and western Asia, precisely like specimens represented on monuments dating from a period of three thousand years ago.

s: musical instruments inform ethnology (as much as they inform musicians)
q: Moreover, a collection of musical instruments deserves the attention of the ethnologist as much as of the musician.

s: musical instruments use material hide of animals (common construction material)
q: Wood, metal, and the hide of animals, are the most common substances used in the construction of musical instruments.

s: musical instruments provide historical evidence (through old specimens and relics)
q: Again, a collection must prove interesting in a historical point of view.

s: Queen Elizabeth is associated with musical instruments (instruments used in England during her time are represented in collections)
q: Scholars will find among old instruments specimens which were in common use in England at the time of queen Elizabeth, and which are not unfrequently mentioned in the literature of that period.

s: musical instruments use material bamboo (especially in tropical countries)
q: In tropical countries bamboo or some similar kind of cane and gourds are especially made use of for this purpose.

s: musical instruments use material gourds (especially in tropical countries)
q: In tropical countries bamboo or some similar kind of cane and gourds are especially made use of for this purpose.

s: musical instruments use material horn (among many vibrating materials)
q: The ingenuity of man has contrived to employ in producing music, horn, bone, glass, pottery, slabs of sonorous stone,--in fact, almost all vibrating matter.

s: musical instruments use material bone (among many vibrating materials)
q: The ingenuity of man has contrived to employ in producing music, horn, bone, glass, pottery, slabs of sonorous stone,--in fact, almost all vibrating matter.

s: M. Lartet surmises use perforated bone whistle (as a hunting whistle)
q: M. Lartet surmises the perforated bone to have been used as a whistle in hunting animals.

s: Poitiers located in France (vicinity of the burial place containing the pipe)
q: was found in a burying-place, dating from the stone period, in the vicinity of Poitiers in France

s: stag-horn pipe is a pipe (rudely made from a fragment of stag's-horn)
q: Another whistle--or rather a pipe, for it has three finger-holes by means of which different tones could be produced--was found in a burying-place, dating from the stone period, in the vicinity of Poitiers in France: it is rudely constructed from a fragment of stag’s-horn.

s: stag-horn pipe has finger holes three (equidistantly placed)
q: It is blown at the end, like a _flûte à bec_ and the three finger-holes are placed equidistantly.

s: stag-horn pipe produces four distinct tones (through its three finger-holes)
q: Four distinct tones must have been easily obtainable on it: the lowest, when all the finger-holes were covered; the other three, by opening the finger-holes successively.

s: stag-horn pipe dates from Stone Age (latest period of the Stone Age)
q: From the character of the stone utensils and weapons discovered with this pipe it is conjectured that the burying-place from which it was exhumed dates from the latest time of the stone age.

s: ancient Egyptians possess ancient Egyptian musical instruments (historically ancient nation)
q: As regards the instruments of the ancient Egyptians we now possess perhaps more detailed information than of those appertaining to any other nation of antiquity.

s: prehistoric musical relics is exhumed in the department of Dordogne in France (recently)
q: A musical relic has recently been exhumed in the department of Dordogne in France, which was constructed in an age when the fauna of France included the reindeer, the rhinoceros, and the mammoth, the hyæna, the bear, and the cave-lion.

s: ancient Egyptian musical instruments are depicted in sculptures and paintings (with notable accuracy)
q: This information we owe especially to the exactness with which the instruments are depicted in sculptures and paintings.

s: ancient Egyptian musical instruments include Egyptian harp (among various instrument types)
q: The Egyptians possessed various kinds of harps, some of which were elegantly shaped and tastefully ornamented.

s: Egyptian harp has height about six and a half feet (largest examples)
q: The largest were about six and a half feet high

s: Egyptian harp is called buni (Egyptian name)
q: The name of the harp was _buni_.

s: Egyptian harp has strings twenty-one (Louvre triangular harp specimen)
q: A kind of triangular harp of the Egyptians was discovered in a well-preserved condition and is now deposited in the Louvre. It has twenty-one strings

s: Egyptian harp deposited in Louvre (well-preserved triangular specimen)
q: A kind of triangular harp of the Egyptians was discovered in a well-preserved condition and is now deposited in the Louvre.

s: James Bruce discovers Egyptian harp (painted in a Theban sepulchre)
q: The Egyptian harps most remarkable for elegance of form and elaborate decoration are the two which were first noticed by Bruce, who found them painted in fresco on the wall of a sepulchre at Thebes

s: Thebes contains Egyptian harp (depicted in a sepulchre fresco)
q: who found them painted in fresco on the wall of a sepulchre at Thebes

s: Rameses III is associated with Thebes (the sepulchre was supposed to be his tomb)
q: supposed to be the tomb of Rameses III. who reigned about 1250 B.C.

s: Dordogne located in France (department)
q: A musical relic has recently been exhumed in the department of Dordogne in France

s: nofre is a guitar (Egyptian instrument)
q: The _nofre_, a kind of guitar, was almost identical in construction with the Tamboura at the present day in use among several eastern nations.

s: nofre has strings two or four (played with a plectrum)
q: The instrument had two or four strings, was played with a plectrum and appears to have been sometimes, if not always, provided with frets.

s: nofre has frets frets (sometimes or always)
q: The instrument had two or four strings, was played with a plectrum and appears to have been sometimes, if not always, provided with frets.

s: British Museum contains some interesting examples (one has seven holes burnt in at the side)
q: There are some interesting examples in the British museum; one of which has seven holes burnt in at the side.

s: Egyptian pipes are made of reed (small pipes with finger-holes)
q: Small pipes of the Egyptians have been discovered, made of reed, with three, four, five, or more finger-holes.

s: Egyptian pipes have finger holes three, four, five, or more (depending on the pipe)
q: Small pipes of the Egyptians have been discovered, made of reed, with three, four, five, or more finger-holes.

s: sêbi is a single flute (of considerable length)
q: The _sêbi_, a single flute, was of considerable length

s: sêbi is made of wood or reed (discovered specimens)
q: Those, however, which have been found are of wood or reed.

s: double-pipe is called mam (popular Egyptian instrument)
q: The Double-Pipe, called _mam_, appears to have been a very popular instrument

s: Egyptian drums are a drum (chiefly barrel-shaped)
q: Furthermore, the Egyptians had, as far as is known to us, two kinds of trumpets; three kinds of tambourines, or little hand drums; three kinds of drums, chiefly barrel-shaped

s: Egyptian drums are covered with parchment (at both ends)
q: The Egyptian drum was from two to three feet in length, covered with parchment at both ends and braced by cords.

s: sistrum is a frame instrument (made of bronze or brass with loose metal bars)
q: The Sistrum consisted of a frame of bronze or brass into which three or four metal bars were loosely inserted, so as to produce a jingling noise when the instrument was shaken.

s: sistrum is used by females (principally in religious performances)
q: The sistrum was principally used by females in religious performances.

s: sistrum is called seshesh (Egyptian name)
q: Its Egyptian name was _seshesh_.

s: perforated bone whistle has material bone (small and less than two inches long)
q: It is a small bone somewhat less than two inches in length, in which is a hole

s: perforated bone whistle has feature artificial hole (bored with a flint knife)
q: It is a small bone somewhat less than two inches in length, in which is a hole, evidently bored by means of one of the little flint knives which men used before acquaintance with the employment of metal for tools and weapons.

s: perforated bone whistle is used as whistle (for hunting animals)
q: M. Lartet surmises the perforated bone to have been used as a whistle in hunting animals.

s: perforated bone whistle is a first digital phalanx of a ruminant (drilled to a certain depth)
q: It is the first digital phalanx of a ruminant, drilled to a certain depth by a smooth cylindrical bore on its lower surface near the expanded upper articulation.

s: perforated bone whistle produces shrill sound (when blown at the lower lip)
q: On applying it to the lower lip and blowing into it a shrill sound is yielded.

s: Assyrian instruments is derived from bas-reliefs (almost entirely)
q: Our acquaintance with the Assyrian instruments has been derived almost entirely from the famous bas-reliefs which have been excavated from the mounds of Nimroud, Khorsabad, and Kouyunjik, situated near the river Tigris in the vicinity of the town of Mosul in Asiatic Turkey.

s: Assyrian harp has strings made of silk (possibly)
q: The strings were perhaps made of silk, like those which the Burmese use at the present time on their harps; or they may have been of catgut, which was used by the ancient Egyptians.

s: Assyrian harp has strings made of catgut (possibly)
q: The strings were perhaps made of silk, like those which the Burmese use at the present time on their harps; or they may have been of catgut, which was used by the ancient Egyptians.

s: Assyrian musicians number eleven performers upon instruments (in the largest assemblage discovered on any monument)
q: The largest assemblage of Assyrian musicians which has been discovered on any monument consists of eleven performers upon instruments, besides a chorus of singers.

s: Assyrian musical procession includes Assyrian harp (played by the first musician, probably the leader)
q: The first musician--probably the leader of the band, as he marches alone at the head of the procession--is playing upon a harp.

s: Assyrian musical procession includes double-pipe (played by one of the second pair of performers)
q: Behind him are two men; one with a dulcimer and the other with a double-pipe: then follow two men with harps.

s: dulcimer is in imperfect state (on the bas-relief)
q: The dulcimer is in too imperfect a state on the bas-relief to familiarize us with its construction.

s: lyre has forms three (on Assyrian bas-reliefs)
q: The Lyre occurs in three different forms, and is held horizontally in playing, or at least nearly so.

s: lyre is held horizontally (in playing, or nearly so)
q: The Lyre occurs in three different forms, and is held horizontally in playing, or at least nearly so.

s: lyre has front bar oblique or slightly curved (generally)
q: Its front bar was generally either oblique or slightly curved.

s: lyre is played with plectrum (as well as with the fingers)
q: The lyre was played with a small plectrum as well as with the fingers.

s: Assyrians use instrumental music for religious observances
q: Instrumental music was used by the Assyrians and Babylonians in their religious observances.

s: Babylonians use instrumental music for religious observances
q: Instrumental music was used by the Assyrians and Babylonians in their religious observances.

s: Nebuchadnezzar commands worship of golden image (when specified instruments sound)
q: Then an herald cried aloud, To you it is commanded, O people, nations, and languages, that at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up.

s: Assyrians maintain musical bands (at royal courts)
q: The kings appear to have maintained at their courts musical bands, whose office it was to perform secular music at certain times of the day or on fixed occasions.

s: Hebrews possess Hebrew musical instruments (known chiefly by biblical names and inferred from Egyptian and Assyrian examples)
q: As regards the musical instruments of the Hebrews, we are from biblical records acquainted with the names of many of them; but representations to be trusted are still wanting, and it is chiefly from an examination of the ancient Egyptian and Assyrian instruments that we can conjecture almost to a certainty their construction and capabilities.

s: harp (Hebrew instrument) is possessed by Hebrews (its biblical name is uncertain)
q: There cannot be a doubt that the Hebrews possessed the harp, seeing that it was a common instrument among the Egyptians and Assyrians. But it is uncertain which of the Hebrew names of the stringed instruments occurring in the Bible really designates the harp.

s: lyre is represented on coins (Hebrew coins generally ascribed to Judas Maccabæus)
q: This instrument is represented on some Hebrew coins generally ascribed to Judas Maccabæus, who lived in the second century before the Christian era.

s: lyre has strings three, five, or six (as shown on Hebrew coins)
q: On three of them are lyres with three strings, another has one with five, and another one with six strings.

s: king David favours kinnor (his favourite instrument, probably a lyre or small triangular harp)
q: The _kinnor_, the favourite instrument of king David, was most likely a lyre if not a small triangular harp.

s: king David maintains royal private band (at Jerusalem)
q: A similar custom prevailed also at the court of Jerusalem, at least in the time of David and Solomon; both of whom appear to have had their royal private bands, besides a large number of singers and instrumental performers of sacred music who were engaged in the Temple.

s: Solomon maintains royal private band (at Jerusalem)
q: A similar custom prevailed also at the court of Jerusalem, at least in the time of David and Solomon; both of whom appear to have had their royal private bands, besides a large number of singers and instrumental performers of sacred music who were engaged in the Temple.

s: Hebrew musical instruments include single pipe (named as the Hebrew single pipe or flute)
q: THE SINGLE PIPE. _Chalil_ and _nekeb_ were the names of the Hebrew pipes or flutes.

s: Assyrian harp is a harp
q: The Assyrian harp was about four feet high, and appears of larger size than it actually was on account of the ornamental appendages which were affixed to the lower part of its frame.

s: bagpipe is denoted by sumphonia (according to Forkel and others)
q: The word _sumphonia_, which occurs in the book of Daniel, is, by Forkel and others, supposed to denote a bagpipe.

s: bagpipe is represented at Tarsus (on an ancient terra-cotta; probably about 2000 years old)
q: Of the real nature of the Hebrew bagpipe perhaps some idea may be formed from a syrinx with bellows, which has been found represented on one of the ancient terra-cottas excavated in Tarsus, Asia-minor, some years since, and here engraved.

s: Hebrews mentions three kinds (in the Bible)
q: Three kinds are mentioned in the Bible, viz. the _keren_, the _shophar_, and the _chatzozerah_.

s: sistrum is denoted by menaaneim (according to Winer, Saalfchütz, and several other commentators)
q: Winer, Saalfchütz, and several other commentators are of opinion that the _menaaneim_, mentioned in 2 Sam. vi. 5, denotes the sistrum.

s: Jubal is father of all such as handle the harp and organ (in Genesis)
q: Jubal is mentioned in Genesis as “the father of all such as handle the harp and organ” (_i.e._, performers on stringed instruments and wind instruments).

s: Jubal is considered first professional cultivator of instrumental music (a possible interpretation)
q: it might perhaps be surmised that Jubal was not regarded as the inventor of all the Hebrew instruments, but rather as the first professional cultivator of instrumental music.

s: Assyrian harp height about four feet
q: The Assyrian harp was about four feet high, and appears of larger size than it actually was on account of the ornamental appendages which were affixed to the lower part of its frame.

s: Bible mentions kinnor (as the oldest stringed instrument and invention of Jubal)
q: The _kinnor_ is mentioned in the Bible as the oldest stringed instrument, and as the invention of Jubal.

s: Old Testament mentions Hebrew musical instruments (about half of the thirty-six instruments recorded by the Rabbins)
q: In the Bible only about half that number are mentioned.

s: Assyrian harp has no front pillar (like Oriental harps)
q: Like all the Oriental harps, modern as well as ancient, it was not provided with a front pillar.

s: Assyrian harp contains sound-holes (in the upper portion of the frame; hour-glass-shaped)
q: The upper portion of the frame contained the sound-holes, somewhat in the shape of an hour-glass.

s: Assyrian harp contains tuning-pegs (below the sound-holes and arranged in regular order)
q: Below them were the screws, or tuning-pegs, arranged in regular order.

s: ancient Greeks derive musical system from Egypt (generally believed)
q: It is generally believed that the Greeks derived their musical system from the Egyptians.

s: lyre is a stringed instrument (Greek instrument class)
q: The Greeks had lyres of various kinds, shown in the accompanying woodcuts, more or less differing in construction, form, and size, and distinguished by different names; such as _lyra, ithara_, _chelys_, _phorminx_, etc.

s: lyre have body shape oval at the base (for one usage of the term lyra)
q: _Lyra_ appears to have implied instruments of this class in general, and also the lyre with a body oval at the base and held upon the lap or in the arms of the performer; while the _kithara_ had a square base and was held against the breast.

s: kithara have base shape square
q: while the _kithara_ had a square base and was held against the breast.

s: kithara be held against breast
q: while the _kithara_ had a square base and was held against the breast.

s: kithara is a three-stringed instrument (of the Lydians)
q: of the three-stringed _kithara_ of the Lydians; and so on.

s: ancient Greeks use kithara (for solo performances)
q: It is recorded that the _kithara_ was employed for solo performances as early as B.C. 700.

s: lyre use strings made of catgut or sinew (strings)
q: The strings, made of catgut or sinew, were more usually twanged with a _plektron_ than merely with the fingers.

s: ancient Greeks derive stringed instruments from Asia (according to the text)
q: but almost all the stringed instruments which the Greeks possessed are stated to have been originally derived from Asia.

s: ancient Greeks use monochord (for teaching singing and acoustics)
q: The _monochord_ had (as its name implies) only a single string, and was used in teaching singing and the laws of acoustics.

s: ancient Greeks use aulos (as a highly popular wind instrument)
q: The flute, _aulos_, of which there were many varieties, as shown in the woodcut p. 31, was a highly popular instrument, and differed in construction from the flutes and pipes of the ancient Egyptians.

s: ancient Greeks use syrinx (Pandean pipe)
q: The _syrinx_, or Pandean pipe, had from three to nine tubes, but seven was the usual number.

s: ancient Greeks use salpinx (exclusively in war)
q: The straight trumpet, _salpinx_, and the curved horn, _keras_, made of brass, were used exclusively in war.

s: ancient Greeks use keras (exclusively in war)
q: The straight trumpet, _salpinx_, and the curved horn, _keras_, made of brass, were used exclusively in war.
